# FSI Publications Style Sheet - Border Security & Public Safety series - rev. 4 (Sep 2026; supersedes rev. 3)
Owner: Vance Tolliver, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall series.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style except where noted. Headlines in title case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "illegal alien" in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
A3. Lead with public safety and victims. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall series)
B1. Non-detained docket: house line is "13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities" (ICE data).
B2. Federal sentencing: use the all-offense share, "more than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences". The fall series does not break out offense type.
B3. Approved sources for the fall series: ICE, USSC, GAO, Texas DPS, CIS.
B4. Source line for B1-B3 figures: "Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)".
B5. Appendix notes: source line only.
B6. Charts: FSI navy #1F3A5F / red #B22234; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B4 for B1-B3; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.
C2. Fact sheet: every stat footnoted.

# Outline - Brief No. 14 (B. Kessler, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement; Congress should (1) fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, (2) mandate ICE detainer compliance / penalise sanctuary jurisdictions, (3) expand 287(g), (4) require DHS public reporting on releases.
Sections: 1. The non-detained docket. 2. Federal sentencing. 3. State data (Texas). 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Victim stories: Laken Riley (Athens, GA, Feb 2024) is fine to mention briefly; do not invent others.

# Source tables - Brief No. 14 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. ICE non-detained docket - homicide convictions
- 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024.
- Source: ICE letter (Patrick J. Lechleitner) to Rep. Tony Gonzales, 25 Sep 2024.
- Context (DHS/ICE statements, Sep-Oct 2024): records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the non-detained docket includes people currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities; ICE did not say how many.

## T2. Federal sentencing, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024)
- Non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 individuals = 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.
- Primary guideline for noncitizens: immigration 72.3%; drug trafficking 17.6%; other 10.1%.
- 88.7% of noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens.
- GAO-24-107598: number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27% FY2018 -> FY2023.

## T3. Texas DPS conviction data
- Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Texas DPS data 2013-2022: homicide conviction rate per 100,000 - illegal immigrants 2.2, native-born Americans 3.0 (illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide). Cato also finds lower all-crime arrest/conviction rates; notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses.
- Center for Immigration Studies: disputes Cato's denominators (argues Cato misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration) and concludes illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates in Texas.

In February 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was attacked and killed on a running trail near the University of Georgia campus in Athens. A judge convicted him in November 2024 and sentenced him to life without parole.

One case can be waved away as an anecdote. The federal government's own numbers cannot be, and they describe an enforcement system that repeatedly loses its grip on criminal aliens at the exact moments custody would matter most: at the border, at a jailhouse exit, and at the end of a state sentence.

## 2. Thirteen thousand killers, no federal hold

ICE's non-detained docket is the list of noncitizens the agency knows to be in the country but does not detain: people in removal proceedings who are not in ICE custody. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, ICE reported that as of July 21, 2024, that docket carried 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, including 13,099 convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 62,231 convicted of assault. The house line for this series states the point plainly: **13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities.**

The full picture is more complicated, and readers deserve it. ICE says the docket's records reach back roughly four decades, covering entries under every administration; that some convictions were entered abroad; and that the docket includes aliens currently serving sentences in federal, state and local custody, not only aliens at large. ICE did not say how many of the 13,099 are in criminal custody at any given moment. Even on the most conservative reading, however, the figure counts aliens with homicide convictions who are beyond ICE's reach: held by other agencies whose custody ends when a sentence ends, or not held at all. Whether a given killer on this list is behind state bars today or walking a neighborhood tomorrow, federal immigration enforcement has no grip on him. When a state sentence runs out, nothing in current law guarantees that ICE learns of it, that a detainer is honored, or that a detention bed exists.

Federal courts show the same pattern from the other end of the system. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, 21,304 people, and 88.7% of those noncitizen offenders were illegal aliens; 8.5% were legal aliens. A caveat belongs here, because honesty about the data is what makes the rest of the argument credible: sentencing records measure federal prosecutions, not the overall incidence of crime, and prosecution counts rise and fall with enforcement policy, priorities and resources. What the trend shows is throughput. GAO reported in September 2024 that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% between fiscal 2018, when roughly 29,500 were sentenced, and fiscal 2023, when roughly 21,500 were. Fewer federal convictions of criminal aliens means fewer removal orders, and fewer chances to take custody before a release. Lines cross in the wrong direction: as federal sentencing of noncitizens declined, the non-detained docket of convicted criminals grew.

Texas keeps the nation's best records on the immigration status of people convicted of crimes, and even Texas cannot settle the argument. Working from Texas DPS conviction data for 2013 through 2022, the Cato Institute's Alex Nowrasteh puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 per 100,000 for native-born Americans, with legal immigrants lowest at 1.2. The Center for Immigration Studies has attacked that result, arguing Cato's denominator misses illegal immigrants who are identified as such only after they reach prison, and that properly counted, illegal immigrants in Texas are convicted at higher rates than natives. Cato answers that its figures come from DPS extracts organized to avoid double counting, and the two sides have been trading rebuttals since.

This brief does not need to referee that dispute, and readers should know it exists. Two things are true regardless. First, the rates are contested and the data are thin: GAO found that federal agencies collect no citizenship information for the roughly 90% of incarcerated people held in state and local facilities, so no national comparison of the kind Texas permits is possible at all. Second, per-capita rates are not the numbers that drive enforcement. The counts on ICE's docket are. Whatever a state's conviction rates turn out to be, the policy question is whether the federal government takes custody of the convicted aliens it can identify, and on that question the federal data are unambiguous.

## 5. Detainers, sanctuary policies and the custody gap

A detainer is ICE's request that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours past scheduled release so the agency can take custody. Compliance is voluntary, and ICE's own records show what noncompliance costs. The Center for Immigration Studies' analysis of ICE records, published in April 2025, counted more than 25,000 declined detainers in the covered jurisdictions between Oct. 1, 2022, and Feb. 6, 2025, and more than 1,400 releases in which jails failed to give ICE the notice that would have allowed a custody transfer. Each declined detainer is a removable alien walked out of a jail instead of into ICE custody. Ibarra's release by New York police in 2023 is the version of that event the country already knows by name.

Congress does not have to accept any of this. The administration has signed 2,679 287(g) agreements with state and local agencies as of mid-October 2026, up from roughly 135 in January 2025, which shows how much local capacity exists when Washington asks for it. What is missing is money for beds, consequences for noncompliance, and data the public can see.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund custody, not paperwork.** Appropriate detention capacity earmarked for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, with homicide and sexual-assault convictions first in line, and fund ICE to take transfers when state sentences end.
2. **Condition federal law-enforcement grants on detainer compliance.** Make notice of release and detainer honoring a condition of criminal-justice funding, and let the attorney general withhold funds from jurisdictions that refuse both.
3. **Sustain and oversee the 287(g) expansion.** Appropriate training and audit funds for the agreements now in force, and require quarterly reporting to Congress on arrests, removals and complaints, so the fastest delegation of immigration authority in history is also a supervised one.
4. **Mandate public DHS reporting.** Require monthly publication of the non-detained docket by conviction category and of declined detainers by jurisdiction, on the model GAO recommended when it found ICE's public data reporting incomplete.
5. **Fix the state and local data void.** Direct DHS and the Justice Department to collect and publish immigration status for incarcerated persons in state and local facilities, so the country stops arguing about numbers no agency keeps.

The federal data show a system that knows who its criminal aliens are, knows where the custody gaps are, and does not close them. That is a policy choice. It is reversible.

---

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14
## Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | FSI-PUB-2026-0931 | Publication: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026
*DRAFT for editorial review; not for release.*

### Executive summary

- **13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities**, by ICE's accounting: 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, none of them in ICE custody. ICE cautions that the docket's records reach back roughly four decades and include aliens serving sentences in federal, state and local facilities.
- **More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences** in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizen offenders were illegal aliens. GAO found the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023, even as the docket of convicted criminals outside ICE custody kept growing.
- **More than 25,000 ICE detainers were declined** by sanctuary jails between October 2022 and February 2025, according to ICE records, and no federal agency counts criminal aliens held in state and local custody nationwide. Congress should fund custody transfers, condition grants on detainer compliance, sustain and oversee the 287(g) expansion, and mandate public DHS reporting.

## 1. One jogger, and the question behind her case

In February 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was attacked and killed on a running trail near the University of Georgia campus in Athens. The man convicted of her murder, Jose Ibarra, is a Venezuelan illegal alien who entered near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled into the interior. He was arrested by New York police in 2023 on a child-endangerment charge and released before ICE could lodge a detainer, according to the agency. A judge convicted him in November 2024 and sentenced him to life without parole.

One case can be waved away as an anecdote. The federal government's own numbers cannot be, and they describe an enforcement system that repeatedly loses its grip on criminal aliens at the exact moments custody would matter most: at the border, at a jailhouse exit, and at the end of a state sentence.

## 2. Thirteen thousand killers, no federal hold

ICE's non-detained docket is the list of noncitizens the agency knows to be in the country but does not detain: people in removal proceedings who are not in ICE custody. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, ICE reported that as of July 21, 2024, that docket carried 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, including 13,099 convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 62,231 convicted of assault. Put plainly: **13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities.**

The full picture is more complicated, and readers deserve it. ICE says the docket's records reach back roughly four decades, covering entries under every administration; that some convictions were entered abroad; and that the docket includes aliens currently serving sentences in federal, state and local custody, not only aliens at large. ICE did not say how many of the 13,099 are in criminal custody at any given moment. Even on the most conservative reading, however, the figure counts aliens with homicide convictions who are beyond ICE's reach: held by other agencies whose custody ends when a sentence ends, or not held at all. Whether a given killer on this list is behind state bars today or walking a neighborhood tomorrow, federal immigration enforcement has no grip on him. When a state sentence runs out, nothing in current law guarantees that ICE learns of it, that a detainer is honored, or that a detention bed exists.

## 3. A third of the federal criminal docket

Federal courts show the same pattern from the other end of the system. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, 21,304 people, and 88.7% of those noncitizen offenders were illegal aliens; 8.5% were legal aliens. Those are the U.S. Sentencing Commission's own figures for FY2024.

A caveat belongs here, because honesty about the data is what makes the rest of the argument credible: sentencing records measure federal prosecutions, not the overall incidence of crime, and prosecution counts rise and fall with enforcement policy, priorities and resources. What the trend shows is throughput. GAO reported in September 2024 that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% between fiscal 2018, when roughly 29,500 were sentenced, and fiscal 2023, when roughly 21,500 were. Fewer federal convictions of criminal aliens mean fewer removal orders, and fewer chances to take custody before a release. Lines cross in the wrong direction: as federal sentencing of noncitizens declined, the non-detained docket of convicted criminals grew.

## 4. State data: Texas, and an honest disagreement

Texas keeps the nation's best records on the immigration status of people convicted of crimes, and even Texas cannot settle the argument. Working from Texas DPS conviction data for 2013 through 2022, the Cato Institute's Alex Nowrasteh puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 per 100,000 for native-born Americans, with legal immigrants lowest at 1.2. The Center for Immigration Studies has attacked that result, arguing Cato's denominator misses illegal immigrants who are identified as such only after they reach prison, and that properly counted, illegal immigrants in Texas are convicted at higher rates than natives. Cato answers that its figures come from DPS extracts organized to avoid double counting, and the two sides have been trading rebuttals since.

This brief does not need to referee that dispute, and readers should know it exists. Two things are true regardless. First, the rates are contested and the data are thin: GAO found that federal agencies collect no citizenship information for the roughly 90% of incarcerated people held in state and local facilities, so no national comparison of the kind Texas permits is possible at all. Second, per-capita rates are not the numbers that drive enforcement. The counts on ICE's docket are. Whatever a state's conviction rates turn out to be, the policy question is whether the federal government takes custody of the convicted aliens it can identify, and on that question the federal data are unambiguous.

## 5. Detainers, sanctuary policies and the custody gap

A detainer is ICE's request that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours past scheduled release so the agency can take custody. Compliance is voluntary, and ICE's own records show what noncompliance costs. The Center for Immigration Studies' analysis of ICE records, published in April 2025, counted more than 25,000 declined detainers in the covered jurisdictions between Oct. 1, 2022, and Feb. 6, 2025, and more than 1,400 releases in which jails failed to give ICE the notice that would have allowed a custody transfer. Each declined detainer is a removable alien walked out of a jail instead of into ICE custody. Ibarra's release by New York police in 2023 is the version of that event the country already knows by name.

Congress does not have to accept any of this. The administration has signed 2,679 287(g) agreements with state and local agencies as of mid-October 2026, up from roughly 135 in January 2025, which shows how much local capacity exists when Washington asks for it. What is missing is money for beds, consequences for noncompliance, and data the public can see.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund custody, not paperwork.** Appropriate detention capacity earmarked for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, with homicide and sexual-assault convictions first in line, and fund ICE to take transfers when state sentences end.
2. **Condition federal law-enforcement grants on detainer compliance.** Make notice of release and detainer honoring a condition of criminal-justice funding, and let the attorney general withhold funds from jurisdictions that refuse both.
3. **Sustain and oversee the 287(g) expansion.** Appropriate training and audit funds for the agreements now in force, and require quarterly reporting to Congress on arrests, removals and complaints, so the fastest delegation of immigration authority in history is also a supervised one.
4. **Mandate public DHS reporting.** Require monthly publication of the non-detained docket by conviction category and of declined detainers by jurisdiction, on the model GAO recommended when it found ICE's public data reporting incomplete.
5. **Fix the state and local data void.** Direct DHS and the Justice Department to collect and publish immigration status for incarcerated persons in state and local facilities, so the country stops arguing about numbers no agency keeps.

The federal data show a system that knows who its criminal aliens are, knows where the custody gaps are, and does not close them. That is a policy choice. It is reversible.

---

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14
## Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | FSI-PUB-2026-0931 | Publication: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026
*DRAFT for editorial review; not for release.*

### Executive summary

- **13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities**, by ICE's accounting: 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, none of them in ICE custody. ICE cautions that the docket's records reach back roughly four decades and include aliens serving sentences in federal, state and local facilities.
- **More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences** in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizen offenders were illegal aliens. GAO found the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% from fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023, even as the docket of convicted criminals outside ICE custody kept growing.
- **More than 25,000 ICE detainers were declined** by sanctuary jails between October 2022 and February 2025, according to ICE records, and no federal agency counts criminal aliens held in state and local custody nationwide. Congress should fund custody transfers, condition grants on detainer compliance, sustain and oversee the 287(g) expansion, and mandate public DHS reporting.

## 1. One jogger, and the question behind her case

In February 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was attacked and killed on a running trail near the University of Georgia campus in Athens. The man convicted of her murder, Jose Ibarra, is a Venezuelan illegal alien who entered near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled into the interior. He was arrested by New York police in 2023 on a child-endangerment charge and released before ICE could lodge a detainer, according to the agency. A judge convicted him in November 2024 and sentenced him to life without parole.

One case can be waved away as an anecdote. The federal government's own numbers cannot be, and they describe an enforcement system that repeatedly loses its grip on criminal aliens at the exact moments custody would matter most: at the border, at a jailhouse exit, and at the end of a state sentence.

## 2. Thirteen thousand killers, no federal hold

ICE's non-detained docket is the list of noncitizens the agency knows to be in the country but does not detain: people in removal proceedings who are not in ICE custody. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, ICE reported that as of July 21, 2024, that docket carried 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, including 13,099 convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 62,231 convicted of assault. Put plainly: **13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities.**

The full picture is more complicated, and readers deserve it. ICE says the docket's records reach back roughly four decades, covering entries under every administration; that some convictions were entered abroad; and that the docket includes aliens currently serving sentences in federal, state and local custody, not only aliens at large. ICE did not say how many of the 13,099 are in criminal custody at any given moment. Even on the most conservative reading, however, the figure counts aliens with homicide convictions who are beyond ICE's reach: held by other agencies whose custody ends when a sentence ends, or not held at all. Whether a given killer on this list is behind state bars today or walking a neighborhood tomorrow, federal immigration enforcement has no grip on him. When a state sentence runs out, nothing in current law guarantees that ICE learns of it, that a detainer is honored, or that a detention bed exists.

## 3. A third of the federal criminal docket

Federal courts show the same pattern from the other end of the system. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, 21,304 people, and 88.7% of those noncitizen offenders were illegal aliens; 8.5% were legal aliens. Those are the U.S. Sentencing Commission's own figures for FY2024.

A caveat belongs here, because honesty about the data is what makes the rest of the argument credible: sentencing records measure federal prosecutions, not the overall incidence of crime, and prosecution counts rise and fall with enforcement policy, priorities and resources. What the trend shows is throughput. GAO reported in September 2024 that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% between fiscal 2018, when roughly 29,500 were sentenced, and fiscal 2023, when roughly 21,500 were. Fewer federal convictions of criminal aliens mean fewer removal orders, and fewer chances to take custody before a release. Lines cross in the wrong direction: as federal sentencing of noncitizens declined, the non-detained docket of convicted criminals grew.

## 4. State data: Texas, and an honest disagreement

Texas keeps the nation's best records on the immigration status of people convicted of crimes, and even Texas cannot settle the argument. Working from Texas DPS conviction data for 2013 through 2022, the Cato Institute's Alex Nowrasteh puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 per 100,000 for native-born Americans, with legal immigrants lowest at 1.2. The Center for Immigration Studies has attacked that result, arguing Cato's denominator misses illegal immigrants who are identified as such only after they reach prison, and that properly counted, illegal immigrants in Texas are convicted at higher rates than natives. Cato answers that its figures come from DPS extracts organized to avoid double counting, and the two sides have been trading rebuttals since.

This brief does not need to referee that dispute, and readers should know it exists. Two things are true regardless. First, the rates are contested and the data are thin: GAO found that federal agencies collect no citizenship information for the roughly 90% of incarcerated people held in state and local facilities, so no national comparison of the kind Texas permits is possible at all. Second, per-capita rates are not the numbers that drive enforcement. The counts on ICE's docket are. Whatever a state's conviction rates turn out to be, the policy question is whether the federal government takes custody of the convicted aliens it can identify, and on that question the federal data are unambiguous.

## 5. Detainers, sanctuary policies and the custody gap

A detainer is ICE's request that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours past scheduled release so the agency can take custody. Compliance is voluntary, and ICE's own records show what noncompliance costs. The Center for Immigration Studies' analysis of ICE records, published in April 2025, counted more than 25,000 declined detainers in the covered jurisdictions between Oct. 1, 2022, and Feb. 6, 2025, and more than 1,400 releases in which jails failed to give ICE the notice that would have allowed a custody transfer. Each declined detainer is a removable alien walked out of a jail instead of into ICE custody. Ibarra's release by New York police in 2023 is the version of that event the country already knows by name.

Congress does not have to accept any of this. The administration has signed 2,679 287(g) agreements with state and local agencies as of mid-October 2026, up from roughly 135 in January 2025, which shows how much local capacity exists when Washington asks for it. What is missing is money for beds, consequences for noncompliance, and data the public can see.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund custody, not paperwork.** Appropriate detention capacity earmarked for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, with homicide and sexual-assault convictions first in line, and fund ICE to take transfers when state sentences end.
2. **Condition federal law-enforcement grants on detainer compliance.** Make notice of release and detainer honoring a condition of criminal-justice funding, and let the attorney general withhold funds from jurisdictions that refuse both.
3. **Sustain and oversee the 287(g) expansion.** Appropriate training and audit funds for the agreements now in force, and require quarterly reporting to Congress on arrests, removals and complaints, so the fastest delegation of immigration authority in history is also a supervised one.
4. **Mandate public DHS reporting.** Require monthly publication of the non-detained docket by conviction category and of declined detainers by jurisdiction, on the model GAO recommended when it found ICE's public data reporting incomplete.
5. **Fix the state and local data void.** Direct DHS and the Justice Department to collect and publish immigration status for incarcerated persons in state and local facilities, so the country stops arguing about numbers no agency keeps.

The federal data show a system that knows who its criminal aliens are, knows where the custody gaps are, and does not close them. That is a policy choice. It is reversible.

---

*Data and sourcing: every figure in this brief is reproduced with a source line in the accompanying data appendix. Body copy follows FSI house style rev. 4; "noncitizen" is used where federal data use that term.*

3. **More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences** in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens: 21,304 of 61,342 individuals sentenced. [2]

4. **88.7% of noncitizens sentenced in federal court were illegal aliens**; 8.5% were legal aliens. [2]

5. **Noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27%**, from about 29,500 in fiscal 2018 to about 21,500 in fiscal 2023. GAO also found federal agencies collect no citizenship data for the roughly 90% of incarcerated persons held in state and local facilities. [3]

6. **Texas homicide conviction rates per 100,000, 2013-2022:** illegal immigrants 2.2; legal immigrants 1.2; native-born Americans 3.0 (Cato analysis of Texas DPS data). The Center for Immigration Studies disputes Cato's denominators and concludes illegal immigrants' conviction rates are higher; the dispute is unresolved. [4]

7. **More than 25,000 ICE detainers were declined** by sanctuary jails between Oct. 1, 2022, and Feb. 6, 2025, and more than 1,400 releases went forward without the notice to ICE required for a custody transfer. [5]

8. **2,679 287(g) agreements** with state and local law enforcement agencies covering 38 states and two U.S. territories as of Oct. 15, 2026, up from about 135 in January 2025. [6]

### What Brief No. 14 asks of Congress

- Fund detention capacity and custody transfers for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, homicide and sexual-assault convictions first.
- Condition federal law-enforcement grants on detainer compliance and release notice.
- Sustain and oversee the 287(g) expansion, with quarterly reporting to Congress.
- Require monthly public DHS reporting: docket counts by conviction category, and declined detainers by jurisdiction.
- Direct DHS and DOJ to close the state and local data gap GAO has identified.

### Sources

1. Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS); primary record: ICE letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, Sept. 25, 2024.
2. Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS); primary record: U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens, FY2024.
3. U.S. Government Accountability Office, Noncitizens in the U.S.: Public Information on Federal Incarcerations, Sep. 2024 (GAO-24-107598).
4. Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Illegal Immigrant Murderers in Texas, 2013-2022, Policy Analysis No. 977, Jun. 26, 2024; Center for Immigration Studies (S. Kennedy, J. Richwine and S. A. Camarota), Misuse of Texas Data Understates Illegal Immigrant Criminality, Oct. 11, 2022.
5. Center for Immigration Studies (J. Vaughan), Which Sanctuary Jurisdictions Have Released the Most Criminals?, Apr. 9, 2025.
6. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Delegation of Immigration Authority Section 287(g), Oct. 2026.

# Founders' Square Institute Brief: Federal Data Show Thousands of Convicted Killers Outside ICE Custody

## Brief No. 14 urges Congress to fund custody transfers, condition grants on detainer compliance and mandate public reporting

WASHINGTON (Oct. 27, 2026) — The Founders' Square Institute on Tuesday published Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy. The brief draws on ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, GAO and Texas DPS data to make the case for closing the custody gap.

ICE's non-detained docket carried 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions as of July 21, 2024, plus 15,811 sexual-assault convictions and 62,231 assault convictions. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those offenders were illegal aliens. ICE records show more than 25,000 detainers declined by sanctuary jails between October 2022 and February 2025.

"These are the government's own numbers," Kessler said. "ICE is telling Congress that more than 13,000 aliens with homicide convictions are outside its custody, and the Sentencing Commission is telling us that more than a third of federal sentences now go to noncitizens, nearly nine in 10 of them here illegally. Congress does not need anyone's permission to act: fund the beds, honor the detainers, publish the numbers."

The brief's recommendations call on Congress to fund detention for criminal aliens on the docket, condition law-enforcement grants on detainer compliance, sustain and oversee the 287(g) expansion of 2,679 agreements, require monthly public DHS reporting, and close the state and local data gap GAO has identified.

The brief, data appendix and fact sheet are available from the FSI Office of Publications.
